teaser: Painted for one man's private rooms, it later earned a mention in a police report.
review_notes:
Image checked: it shows Le Sommeil (Petit Palais), signed and dated '66 at lower right, with a decorative border from the photograph's frame at the edges.
Size 135 x 200 cm.
1866 context: Salon success with Woman with a Parrot and Covert of Roe Deer; Courbet was 47 (born June 1819).
Commission by Khalil Bey after he failed to obtain Venus and Psyche (1864): standard account. The price of 20,000 francs is often cited but is NOT stated in the lesson.
Khalil Bey also owned Ingres's Turkish Bath, and sold his collection in 1868 after gambling losses.
Red-haired model identified as Joanna Hiffernan, Whistler's companion: widely repeated but not proven; lesson says 'probably'.
1872 police report when a dealer displayed the picture: please verify.
Link to Baudelaire's banned poems of 1857 (Femmes damnees): a common art-historical suggestion.
Entered the Petit Palais in 1953.

lesson.text: By 1866 Gustave Courbet was 47, heavy, loud and, for the first time, fashionable. The man who had spent the 1850s fighting juries now had two hits at the Paris Salon in a single spring. Dealers wrote to him. Rich clients asked for seascapes, deer in the snow, nudes. He was earning more than he ever had.

Success brought a new kind of customer. Khalil Bey was a diplomat from the Ottoman Empire, living in Paris in great style, a gambler and a serious collector. He had seen a Courbet picture of two women that he wanted badly, but it was already sold. Courbet offered to paint him something else along the same lines. This is it.

Khalil Bey's collection was built around the female body. He owned The Turkish Bath by Ingres, a round canvas crowded with nudes, and he kept his most daring pictures in private rooms shown only to chosen guests.

So Sleep was never meant for a public wall. That matters for how to read it. A Salon nude of the time had to wear an alibi: call her Venus or a nymph, set her in a forest, and nakedness became respectable. Here there is no alibi. Two modern women sleep in a modern bedroom, at life scale, on a canvas two meters wide (about 6 and a half feet).
What made a nude acceptable in 1866 was distance: a myth, a far-off land, an ancient time. Courbet removes the distance and paints the present.

He also paints it very well, and that is the other half of the story. Courbet treats the picture as a contest of whites and skin tones. Put one body beside another, both beside linen, all of it against a deep blue hanging, and each color has to be found exactly or the whole thing turns to chalk.

The two women are not twins, and he uses the difference. One has dark hair and cooler, paler skin. The other is a redhead with a warmer, pinker tone. Then come the things scattered around the bed. They are not decoration. Read in order, they tell you what the evening was like before the room went quiet.

lesson.title: Evidence
lesson.text: Three clues left on and around the bed.

spots.title: The broken necklace
spots.text: A string of pearls trails across the sheet from under the dark-haired woman's arm, its thread snapped. Jewelry that breaks is jewelry that was pulled.

spots.title: The comb
spots.text: On the far side of the bed lie a gold hair comb and a few loose pearls. Hair has come undone, and nobody stopped to pick anything up.

spots.title: The night table
spots.text: A blue glass decanter, a stemmed cup and a crystal vase stand on a lacquered table. Luxury objects, painted with a still-life painter's care: this is a wealthy woman's room.

lesson.text: A snapped necklace, a lost comb, a drink within reach. Courbet shows nothing but sleep, and lets the objects speak about what came before. For his buyer this was the appeal. For the history of painting it was a quiet shift: love between two women treated as a subject from daily life, without monsters, punishment or moral.

The redhead is probably Joanna Hiffernan, an Irish model and the companion of the American painter James McNeill Whistler. Courbet had met the couple by the sea in Normandy the summer before and painted her combing that copper hair.

Poetry had been here first. In 1857 Charles Baudelaire, whom Courbet knew well, had been taken to court over a book of poems, and several of the condemned pieces dealt with women who love women. Courbet's canvas is often read as an answer in paint to his friend's banned verses.

spots.title: Two heads
spots.text: The redhead's face nestles against the other woman's shoulder. Dark curls spill left over the pillow, copper ones right: Courbet sets the two colors side by side like samples.

spots.title: The resting hand
spots.text: A hand lies loosely on a leg, fingers relaxed. Courbet is careful to paint limbs with real weight. These bodies press into the mattress and into each other.

spots.title: The flowers
spots.text: A porcelain vase of orange, red and white flowers glows against the dark. It is the one hot spot of color in the picture, placed far from the faces to balance them.

spots.title: The blue hanging
spots.text: A heavy midnight-blue curtain closes off the room. Blue is the opposite of orange-pink, so it makes the skin look warmer than it would against any other color.

spots.title: The sheets
spots.text: White linen, then a pink cover sliding off the bed. Courbet lays the paint on thickly here, in broad strokes that follow each fold, so the cloth has almost as much body as the skin.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: Signed and dated in red at the corner: G. Courbet, 66. He put his name on a picture many colleagues would have left unsigned.

lesson.text: The private rooms did not last. Khalil Bey lost his fortune at the gaming tables and sold his collection in 1868. Sleep passed to other owners, and when a dealer dared to put it on view a few years later, the police took note of it in a report.

It took until 1953 for the painting to enter a public museum, the Petit Palais in Paris, almost ninety years after Courbet signed it. Today it hangs there in an ordinary gallery, and school groups walk past.

quiz.question: Who was Sleep painted for?
options: A private collector, the Ottoman diplomat Khalil Bey
quiz.explanation: Khalil Bey commissioned it for his private rooms.

quiz.question: What usually made a nude acceptable to the public in 1866?
quiz.explanation: Calling the figure Venus or a nymph gave nakedness an excuse, which Courbet refuses here.

quiz.question: What trails across the sheet near the dark-haired woman's arm?
quiz.explanation: The snapped string of pearls hints at what happened before they slept.

quiz.question: Why does the blue curtain matter for the color of the skin?
options: It reflects blue light onto the bodies
Blue is the opposite of orange-pink, so the skin looks warmer
quiz.explanation: The contrast with deep blue makes the flesh tones glow.

quiz.question: What was Courbet's situation in 1866?
options: He was in exile and poor
He was successful and in demand
quiz.explanation: After two Salon hits that spring, dealers and wealthy clients were seeking him out.

facts.text: Sleep was first shown to large crowds at the Paris Salon.
facts.explanation: It was made for a collector's private rooms, not for public exhibition.

facts.text: The painting only entered a public museum in 1953.
facts.explanation: The Petit Palais acquired it almost ninety years after it was painted.

facts.text: The two sleeping women are presented as Greek goddesses.
facts.explanation: They are modern women in a modern bedroom, with no mythological excuse.
